<STRUCT_0001>
The following result says that a Deligne-Mumford stack whose inertia
is trivial ``is'' an algebraic space. This lemma will be obsoleted by
the stronger
Proposition <REF_0001>
below which says that this holds more generally for algebraic stacks...

Let <MATH_0001> be a scheme contained in <MATH_0002>.
Let <MATH_0003> be an algebraic stack over <MATH_0004>.
The following are equivalent
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> <MATH_0005> is a Deligne-Mumford stack and is a stack in setoids,
<STRUCT_0003> <MATH_0006> is a Deligne-Mumford stack such that the
canonical <MATH_0007>-morphism <MATH_0008>
is an equivalence, and
<STRUCT_0004> <MATH_0009> is representable by an algebraic space.
<STRUCT_0005>

The equivalence of (1) and (2) follows from
Stacks, Lemma <REF_0001>.
The implication (3) <MATH_0001> (1) follows from
Lemma <REF_0002>.
Finally, assume (1). By
Stacks, Lemma <REF_0003>
there exists a sheaf <MATH_0002> on <MATH_0003>
and an equivalence <MATH_0004>. By
Lemma <REF_0004>
the fact that <MATH_0005> is representable by algebraic
spaces, means that <MATH_0006>
is representable by algebraic spaces.
Let <MATH_0007> be a scheme, and let <MATH_0008>
be a surjective <ACCENT_0001>tale morphism. The composition
<MATH_0009>
corresponds to a morphism <MATH_0010> of sheaves. By
Bootstrap, Lemma <REF_0005>
this morphism is representable by algebraic spaces.
Hence by
Lemma <REF_0006>
we conclude that <MATH_0011> is surjective and <ACCENT_0002>tale.
Finally, we apply
Bootstrap, Theorem <REF_0007>
to see that <MATH_0012> is an algebraic space.
